paragraphs: “But how could we not be friendly to you?” said my hostess, laughing. The room was full of people. All at once the young lady rose, the one the duel had been fought over, the one I had only lately meant to make my wife. I had not noticed her come into the room. She got up, came over to me and held out her hand.
“Let me tell you,” she said, “that I am the first who does not laugh at you. On the contrary, I thank you with tears, and I respect you for what you did then.”

Her husband came up too, and then they all crowded round me and nearly kissed me. My heart was full of joy. But my attention was caught above all by a middle-aged man who came up with the others. I already knew him by name, but I had never met him or exchanged a word with him until that evening.
_(d) The Mysterious Visitor_

He had been an official in our town for many years. He held a prominent position, was respected by everyone, was rich, and had a name for kindness. He gave large sums to the almshouse and the orphanage. He was very generous in secret too, which only became known after his death. He was about fifty, almost stern to look at, and not much of a talker. He had been married about ten years, and his wife, who was still young, had given him three children. Well, the following evening I was sitting alone in my room when the door suddenly opened and this gentleman walked in.

I should mention, by the way, that I no longer lived in my old quarters. As soon as I resigned my commission, I took rooms with an old lady, the widow of a government clerk. Her servant looked after me. I had moved into her house simply because, on coming back from the duel, I had sent Afanasy back to the regiment. I was ashamed to look him in the face after my last talk with him. That is how ready a man of the world is to be ashamed of any righteous act.

“I have been listening to you with great interest,” said my visitor, “in several houses these last few days, and I wanted at last to make your personal acquaintance, so that we could talk more intimately. Can you, dear sir, do me this favor?”

“I can, with the greatest pleasure, and I shall count it an honor.” I said this, though I felt almost dismayed, so strongly did this man impress me from the first moment. Others had listened to me with interest and attention, but no one had ever come to me with such a serious, stern and concentrated look. And now he had come to see me in my own rooms. He sat down.
“You are, I see, a man of great strength of character,” he said, “since you dared to serve the truth even when you risked everyone’s contempt by doing so.”
“Perhaps you praise me too much,” I replied.

“No, it is not too much,” he answered. “Believe me, what you did is far harder than you think. That is what struck me, and that alone is why I have come to you,” he went on. “Tell me, please, if my perhaps improper curiosity does not annoy you, what exactly did you feel, if you can recall it, at the moment when you made up your mind to ask forgiveness at the duel? Do not think my question idle. On the contrary, I have a secret reason of my own for asking, which I may explain to you later, if it is God’s will that we come to know each other better.”
All the while he spoke I was looking straight into his face, and I felt all at once that I trusted him completely. I was very curious too, for I sensed that there was some strange secret in his soul.

“You ask what exactly I felt at the moment I asked my opponent’s forgiveness,” I answered. “But I had better tell you from the beginning something I have not yet told anyone.” And I described everything that had passed between Afanasy and me, and how I had bowed down to the ground at his feet. “From that you can see for yourself,” I finished, “that at the time of the duel it was easier for me. I had already made a beginning at home. And once I had started down that road, going further along it was not hard at all, but became a source of joy and happiness.”
I liked the way he looked at me as he listened. “All that,” he said, “is extremely interesting. I will come to see you again and again.”

And from then on he came to see me nearly every evening. We might have become closer friends, if only he had ever talked about himself. But he hardly ever said a word about himself, while he kept asking me about myself. Even so, I grew very fond of him and spoke to him with perfect frankness about all my feelings. “For,” I thought, “what need do I have to know his secrets, when I can see without it that he is a good man? Besides, serious as he is, and older than I am, he comes to visit a youngster like me and treats me as his equal.” And I learned a great deal from him that was useful, for he was a man of lofty mind.

“That life is heaven,” he said to me suddenly, “is something I have long been thinking about”; and then he added all at once, “Indeed, I think of nothing else.” He looked at me and smiled. “I am more convinced of it than you are. I will tell you later why.”
I listened to him and thought that he evidently wanted to tell me something.
“Heaven,” he went on, “lies hidden within each one of us. Here it lies hidden in me now, and if I will it, it will be revealed to me tomorrow and for all time.”
I looked at him. He was speaking with great emotion and gazing at me mysteriously, as if he were questioning me.

“And that we are all responsible to all and for all, besides our own sins, you were quite right to think so, and it is wonderful that you could grasp it in its full meaning at once. And in very truth, as soon as men understand that, the Kingdom of Heaven will be for them not a dream but a living reality.”
“And when,” I cried out to him bitterly, “when will that come about? And will it ever come about? Is it not simply a dream of ours?”

“What, then, you do not believe it?” he said. “You preach it and do not believe it yourself. Believe me, this dream, as you call it, will come to pass without doubt. It will come, but not now, for every process has its law. This is a spiritual, psychological process. To transform the world, to make it over anew, men must turn onto another path psychologically. Until you have become a brother to everyone, really and in fact, brotherhood will not come. No kind of scientific teaching, no common interest, will ever teach men to share property and privileges with equal regard for all. Everyone will think his share too small, and they will always be envying, complaining and attacking one another. You ask when it will come to pass. It will come to pass, but first we have to go through the period of isolation.”
“What do you mean by isolation?” I asked him.

“Why, the isolation that prevails everywhere, above all in our age. It has not fully developed yet, it has not reached its limit. For everyone strives to keep his individuality as separate as possible and wants to secure the greatest possible fullness of life for himself. But meanwhile all his efforts end not in fullness of life but in self-destruction, for instead of finding himself he ends by arriving at complete solitude. All mankind in our age has split up into separate units. They all keep apart, each in his own groove. Each one holds himself aloof, hides himself and hides what he has from the rest, and he ends by being repelled by others and repelling them. He heaps up riches by himself and thinks, ‘How strong I am now, and how secure.’ In his madness he does not understand that the more he heaps up, the deeper he sinks into self-destroying helplessness. For he is used to relying on himself alone and cutting himself off from the whole. He has trained himself not to believe in the help of others, in men and in humanity, and he only trembles for fear of losing his money and the privileges he has won for himself. Everywhere in these days men have, in their mockery, stopped understanding that true security is to be found in social solidarity rather than in isolated individual effort. But this terrible individualism must inevitably come to an end, and all will suddenly understand how unnaturally they are separated from one another. It will be the spirit of the time, and people will marvel that they sat so long in darkness without seeing the light. And then the sign of the Son of Man will be seen in the heavens.... But until then we must keep the banner flying. Sometimes, even if he has to do it alone and his conduct seems crazy, a man must set an example, and so draw men’s souls out of their solitude and spur them to some act of brotherly love, so that the great idea may not die.”

Our evenings, one after another, were spent in such stirring and fervent talk. I gave up society and visited my neighbors much less often. Besides, my vogue was somewhat over. I say this not as a reproach, for they still loved me and treated me good-humoredly, but there is no denying that fashion is a great power in society. I began to regard my mysterious visitor with admiration. Besides enjoying his intelligence, I began to see that he was brooding over some plan in his heart and was perhaps preparing himself for a great deed. Perhaps he liked it that I showed no curiosity about his secret and did not try to discover it by a direct question or by hints. But at last I noticed that he seemed to show signs of wanting to tell me something. This had become quite plain about a month after he first began to visit me.
“Do you know,” he said to me once, “that people in the town are very curious about us, and wonder why I come to see you so often? But let them wonder, for _soon all will be explained_.”

Sometimes an extraordinary agitation would come over him, and almost always on such occasions he would get up and go away. Sometimes he would fix a long, piercing look on me, and I thought, “He will say something right now.” But he would suddenly begin talking of something ordinary and familiar. He often complained of headache too.
One day, quite unexpectedly, after he had been talking with great fervor for a long time, I saw him suddenly turn pale. His face worked convulsively, while he stared fixedly at me.
“What is the matter?” I said. “Do you feel ill?” He had just been complaining of headache.
“I ... do you know ... I murdered someone.”
He said this and smiled, with a face as white as chalk. “Why is he smiling?” The thought flashed through my mind before I understood anything else. I too turned pale.
“What are you saying?” I cried.
“You see,” he said, with a pale smile, “how much it has cost me to say the first word. Now that I have said it, I feel I have taken the first step, and I shall go on.”

For a long while I could not believe him, and I did not believe him at that time. I believed him only after he had come to see me three days running and told me all about it. I thought he was mad, but I ended by being convinced, to my great grief and amazement. His crime was a great and terrible one.

Fourteen years before, he had murdered the widow of a landowner, a wealthy and handsome young woman who had a house in our town. He fell passionately in love with her, declared his feeling and tried to persuade her to marry him. But she had already given her heart to another man, an officer of noble birth and high rank in the service, who was at that time away at the front, though she expected him to return soon. She refused his offer and begged him not to come and see her. After he stopped visiting her, he used his knowledge of the house to get in at night through the garden by way of the roof, at great risk of being discovered. But, as often happens, a crime committed with extraordinary audacity succeeds better than others.

He got into the garret through the skylight and went down the ladder. He knew that the door at the bottom was sometimes left unlocked through the carelessness of the servants. He hoped to find it so, and so it was. He made his way in the dark to her bedroom, where a light was burning. As though on purpose, both her maids had gone off without asking leave to a birthday party in the same street. The other servants slept in the servants’ quarters or in the kitchen on the ground floor. His passion flamed up at the sight of her asleep, and then vindictive, jealous anger took possession of his heart. Like a drunken man, beside himself, he thrust a knife into her heart, so that she did not even cry out. Then, with devilish and criminal cunning, he arranged things so that suspicion would fall on the servants. He was base enough to take her purse, to open her chest with keys from under her pillow and take some things from it, doing it all as an ignorant servant might have done it, leaving valuable papers and taking only money. He took some of the larger gold things, but left smaller articles that were ten times as valuable. He also took some things for himself as keepsakes, but of that later. Having done this awful deed, he went back the way he had come.

Neither the next day, when the alarm was raised, nor at any time later in his life, did anyone dream of suspecting him of the crime. No one, indeed, knew of his love for her, for he was always reserved and silent and had no friend to whom he would have opened his heart. He was looked on simply as an acquaintance of the murdered woman, and not a close one, since for the previous fortnight he had not even visited her. A serf of hers called Pyotr was at once suspected, and every circumstance confirmed the suspicion. The man knew, and indeed his mistress had not hidden it, that she had to send one of her serfs as a recruit and had decided to send him, since he had no relations and his conduct was unsatisfactory. People had heard him angrily threatening to murder her when he was drunk in a tavern. Two days before her death he had run away, and no one knew where in the town he stayed. The day after the murder he was found on the road leading out of the town, dead drunk, with a knife in his pocket, and his right hand happened to be stained with blood. He declared that his nose had been bleeding, but no one believed him. The maids confessed that they had gone to a party and that the street door had been left open until they came back. And a number of similar details came to light, all throwing suspicion on the innocent servant.

They arrested him, and he was tried for the murder. But a week after his arrest the prisoner fell sick with a fever and died unconscious in the hospital. There the matter ended. The judges, the authorities and everyone in the town remained convinced that the crime had been committed by no one but the servant who had died in the hospital. And after that the punishment began.

My mysterious visitor, now my friend, told me that at first he was not troubled in the least by pangs of conscience. He was miserable for a long time, but not for that reason. It was only regret that he had killed the woman he loved, that she was no more, that in killing her he had killed his love, while the fire of passion was still in his veins. But of the innocent blood he had shed, of the murder of a fellow creature, he scarcely thought. The thought that his victim might have become the wife of another man was unbearable to him, and so for a long time he was convinced in his conscience that he could not have acted otherwise.

At first he was worried by the arrest of the servant, but the man’s illness and death soon set his mind at rest. For the man’s death was apparently (so he reflected at the time) not due to his arrest or his fright, but to a chill he had caught on the day he ran away, when he had lain all night dead drunk on the damp ground. The theft of the money and other things troubled him little, for he argued that the theft had not been committed for gain but to turn away suspicion. The sum stolen was small, and shortly afterwards he gave the whole of it, and much more, to the funds for maintaining an almshouse in the town. He did this on purpose to set his conscience at rest about the theft, and it is a remarkable fact that for a long time he really was at peace. He told me this himself. He then entered on a career of great activity in the service. He volunteered for a difficult and laborious duty, which occupied him two years, and being a man of strong will he almost forgot the past. Whenever he recalled it, he tried not to think of it at all. He became active in philanthropy too, founded and helped to maintain many institutions in the town, did a good deal in the two capitals, and was elected a member of philanthropic societies in both Moscow and Petersburg.
